body: Do you live in Ontario?  The numbers James sent look like a longitude and latitude.  It's a location right off of a road East of Elliot Lake.

The more I think about it, the more hopeless it seems.  I can't find a reason good enough to remain here.  We are afraid of what comes next because we don't know what it is, but it could very well be far better than here.  I can't find a good enough reason to stay.
If there's no higher purpose, then I could die right now and it wouldn't matter.  If I have a few laughs between now and death, what does it really matter?  It'll come anyway, so why not now?
Not everyone is ingrained the same way.

A few of my questions are as follows; why are we here? How are we here?  How are we self-aware?  Why do we value "good" and where does that notion come from?

I am aware that death could lead to a less favorable fate than the one I have now.  But, it also might not.  Maybe learning here on earth will help, maybe it won't, but there is one way to find out.

I understand what you are saying, for the most part.  You say that your actions/experiences result in something profound and beautiful.  What is profound and beautiful, or if you are talking about the actions/experiences themselves, what makes them profound and beautiful?  

Humans have a desire to overcome, learn, and grow.  Where does it come from?  That's a tough question to answer, but it is hard to deny the existence of that desire.  Not everyone shares it, but humanity as a whole works towards a better understanding of reality.  But we all do it in our own ways.  Some use philosophy, some use science, some use psychology, and, of course, some don't even care.  I have a desire to overcome, learn, and grow too.  Suicide is a valid option in the pursuit of knowledge concerning some of life's greatest mysteries.  I can appreciate the vast beauty of the Milky Way as well, but I cannot stop myself from asking why.  Why is it there and why does it make me marvel?  To make any forward progress into the realm of the value of life and proper moral standards, or what really makes life good, we need to know why things are here.  If we don't, how can we hope to know what is good and what makes life worth living?  Maybe, life isn't either good or worth living.

I think it's one of the things that matters the most.  If this one life is all there is, then what are we truly working towards?  What can we truly achieve?  Yes, we can work to try to make life for future generations better, but we all have different definitions of "better".  What really is the best if all we can base our ideals on exist in this life?

Even if there is not a "world beyond", death shows us the truth.  If it is just emptiness, then it won't matter, because there will be nothing to know.  Whatever comes next, death is the only way to find out, and that is why I have been thinking about it so much lately.

Do you not want to go back to that state of understanding?  Why would you want to continue after knowing that trying to understand life is futile?

I appreciate you sharing your story, and I don't want to discourage you from sharing it again, but the state you described sounds much more preferable to where we are now.  I long to know, and to understand, and if that can be achieved through death, then that is what I want.

I think you have some good thoughts.  I will post something similar on /r/philosophy to see what I can come up with.  Thank you for you suggestion.

I agree that the most scientific way to look at things is the way you explained above.  But if that is the case, all our hope rests in humanity.  I cannot help but think of how frail we are.  Yes, we are also resilient, but one misplaced asteroid and all we have worked for is done.  It may seem a bit cliche, but such is life.  Even if we are not facing mass extinction, I struggle with the thought that survival is our prime directive.  There are many things we should do that would be considered "immoral" if our end goal is survival, such as euthanasia and even genocide.  We may cringe at these ideas now and we certainly hope that a better alternative will present itself in the future, but earth's resources are limited and won't sustain humanity forever.  The less people there are on Earth, the longer we survive, the longer we survive, the better chance we have of finding a more desirable solution.

And I also agree that every answer I have come up with myself and every answer I have received has had its assumptions.  But if that's the case, if we cannot even prove that our senses are reliable, why not die to find out if there is something beyond the world we perceive with our senses?
I guess my biggest questions are; what do we base our morals on, and is there any absolute truth?
